co_ironing_board_slabs_upper_lower_slabs.blurb: A roadside set of stacked slabs in the narrow stretch of Big Thompson Canyon, reached from a pullout a little over half a mile up-canyon from the beige siphon tube. The cliff is built in four tiers and holds sixteen climbs, mostly trad with a handful of bolted lines and one low traverse problem. Difficulty centres on 5.9 and 5.10, with a few easier pitches around 5.7 and 5.8 and one 5.11. Several lines are run-out or only partly protected, and gear tends to be small, so this suits climbers comfortable placing their own protection. A couple of routes stretch to two pitches.

co_mind_matters_boulder.blurb: One very large boulder at the far end of the trail through the 7 Mile Boulders, high on Guanella Pass above Georgetown at roughly 10,400 feet. Beyond the main warm-up area and the Bessie boulder, it is the last big block you meet. Sixteen problems wrap nearly every side, with a spread from V3 up through V13: a few moderate and mid-grade lines, then a dense cluster of hard V10 to V12 testpieces. The landing is less friendly than at neighbouring boulders, so bring several pads and spotters. Sub-alpine setting, so expect cool temperatures.

co_waffle_house.blurb: A compact crag in the West Valley sector of Devil's Head in the South Platte, set just beneath the fire tower. Sixteen routes, thirteen of them bolted and three trad, run from roughly 65 to 90 feet. Most of the grades sit between 5.6 and 5.10, which makes it a comfortable spot for newer leaders, with a few 5.11 and one 5.12 above. The granite offers a variety: cracks, chickenheads, technical face and some slab. It catches sun and shade through much of the day and goes entirely into shade late in the afternoon.

co_vasquez_road.blurb: A small, spread-out bouldering zone beside Vasquez Road in the Fraser Valley, a short drive from Winter Park at about 9,200 feet. Sixteen problems are scattered across a few boulders, including the Water Station, Jellyfish and Pinball blocks, some just steps from the road and others a ten-minute woodland walk. The grades are friendly: from very easy up to V4, with most falling between V0 and V3, so it works well for beginners and warm-ups. Forest surrounds the boulders and further lines remain to be found among the trees. Mountain bikers share some trails.

co_third_buttress.blurb: The third of the Elephant Buttresses in Boulder Canyon, a trad-only face with sixteen one- and two-pitch routes and no bolts. Grades start around 5.7 and climb to a handful of 5.11s, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.10 and the harder lines clustered at 5.11. Climbers describe the rock as solid, and the long moderate lines make it a popular objective for those building up multi-pitch trad. Routes start either from a gully beside the neighbouring buttress or directly off the water pipe that serves as the approach path. The common descent is an exposed downclimb best avoided by beginners.

co_super_sector.blurb: The central amphitheater of the Fortress of Solitude, a big limestone sport cliff near New Castle at roughly 6,400 feet. Sixteen bolted lines here mostly sit in the 5.13 to 5.14 range, with just one at 5.11 and one reaching 5.15. This is serious, steep climbing, and routes often feel harder than they look from below. Reaching it takes a long uphill effort: a trail through Hadley Gulch followed by a talus slope, close to an hour overall. Much of the cliff is lightly travelled, and the lowest stretch of many routes can sit on a loose shaley band.
co_super_sector.approach: Follow the Hadley Gulch trail for around half an hour, then work up a talus field, staying left along the roped trail to the amphitheater.

co_upper_wall_the_2.blurb: The upper tier of First Buttress in Taylor Canyon near Gunnison, a large wall holding sixteen mostly trad lines. Difficulty spreads from 5.7 through 5.10 to a few 5.11 and one 5.12, with many sustained and demanding pitches and a sport line or two. Granite, early morning sun and afternoon shade, so it is pleasant on warm days. Reach it by scrambling up from the corner below, then follow a ledge system along the base to the left and middle routes. Small wired nuts are useful on the thinner cracks.
